nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Oxford Movement and Victorian religious prose
literary_identity: Priest, fellow of Oriel and Tractarian controversialist; the ascetic and fiery early influence of the Oxford Movement, whose Remains became the scandal and the manifesto of the Tracts.
biography: Born at Dartington on 25 March 1803, son of the archdeacon of Totnes; educated at Eton and Oriel College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1826 and met Newman and Keble. He wrote some of the first Tracts for the Times, travelled with Newman in the Mediterranean in 1832-33 (where the poems of Lyra Apostolica were written), and was perpetually ill; he was ordained in 1829 and appointed archdeacon of Totnes in 1830. He died of tuberculosis at Dartington on 28 February 1836, aged thirty-two. Newman published his Remains in 1838-39, and their extreme opinions on the Reformation caused a controversy that helped both to define and to divide the Oxford Movement.
literary_profile: Froude supplied the Oxford Movement with its ascetic ideal and its historical theory: he was a High Churchman who believed the Church of England had been corrupted at the Reformation, and his biography of Becket set the martyr and the king in the pattern that his successors repeated. The Remains, with their journals and letters, present a personality of radical earnestness and self-mortification, and their publication was the moment at which the movement's extreme wing became visible.
stylistic_characteristics: Personal journals and letters as devotional documents; unqualified assertion and the polemical aside; a historical argument that treats the Reformation as a national apostasy; the aphorism and the ascetic self-examination.
intellectual_concerns: The authority of the Church against the state; apostolic succession and the eucharistic sacrifice; asceticism, fasting and celibacy; the corruption of the sixteenth-century settlement; the relation of the Anglican Church to Rome.
historical_significance: Froude's Remains made the Oxford Movement visible as a party and provoked the critical reaction that produced the 1841 Tract 90 crisis and, finally, Newman's secession. He is the movement's intimate historian, and his influence on Newman, Keble and Pusey was the decisive personal influence of its first decade.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Lyra Apostolica (contributor, 1836); Tracts for the Times, no. 4 and no. 9 (1833); Remains of the Late Reverend Richard Hurrell Froude (posthumous, 2 vols, 1838-39); The Life of the Blessed St Thomas Becket (in the Remains); Sermons and correspondence (in the Remains).

literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the inventor of the English sensation novel and of the modern detective story.
biography: Born in London on 8 January 1824, son of the landscape painter William Collins. He was educated privately in Italy and at Lincoln's Inn, where he was called to the bar in 1851 but never practised. He met Dickens in 1851 and became his friend, collaborator and contributor to Household Words and All the Year Round. Antonina (1850) was his first novel; The Woman in White (serialised 1859-60) made him famous and The Moonstone (1868) invented the English detective novel. From the 1860s he suffered from rheumatic gout and became dependent on laudanum, and he lived with two households, a wife and a mistress, in a domestic arrangement that Victorian society did not acknowledge. He died in London on 23 September 1889.
literary_profile: Collins took the Gothic machinery of the 1790s — the asylum, the forged will, the substituted identity, the secret in the family — and moved it into contemporary England and English law. His great innovation is the multiple-narrator method: the story is told in turn by the witnesses and participants, each with a limited and interested view, and the reader must assemble the truth from their testimony. He wrote as a lawyer's son about the legal position of women (the woman in white has no name, no property and no credibility), and as a professional novelist about the new class of doctors, clerks and detectives.
stylistic_characteristics: Documentary narration through letters, diaries and witness statements; the withholding of information by a narrator with a reason to withhold it; precise legal and medical detail; doubles, substituted identities and mistaken names; a plot built on the exact sequence of evidence; short chapters and serial climaxes.
intellectual_concerns: Identity and the legal person; marriage, coverture and the property of women; madness, confinement and the asylum; class and the professional middle class; empire and the colonial secret; crime and the limits of the law; the double life of the respectable Victorian.
historical_significance: Collins invented the English sensation novel and, with The Moonstone, the English detective novel; his multiple-narrator method is the model for the whole modern literature of testimony, from Conrad to the contemporary crime novel. His treatment of women's legal non-existence helped to make the Married Women's Property Acts arguable, and his novels are now read as the central case of Victorian popular fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Victorian novel and poetry
literary_identity: Novelist and poet; the most intellectually demanding of the Victorian novelists and the author of Modern Love and The Egoist.
biography: Born at Portsmouth on 12 February 1828, the grandson of a naval outfitter; his mother died when he was five and he was sent to a Moravian school in Germany at fourteen. He was articled to a solicitor in London in 1845, married Mary Ellen Nicolls — the widowed daughter of Thomas Love Peacock — in 1849, and was left by her in 1858 for the painter Henry Wallis; she died in 1861, and Modern Love (1862) is the record of the marriage. He worked as a publisher's reader for Chapman and Hall (the first reader of Far from the Madding Crowd) and as a journalist, and married Marie Vulliamy in 1864. The Ordeal of Richard Feverel (1859) began his career; Emilia in England (1864), Rhoda Fleming (1865), The Adventures of Harry Richmond (1871), Beauchamp's Career (1876), The Egoist (1879), Diana of the Crossways (1885), One of Our Conquerors (1891) and The Amazing Marriage (1895) followed. He received the Order of Merit in 1905 and died at Box Hill on 18 May 1909.
literary_profile: Meredith wrote the English novel of comedy in the high, philosophic sense: his subject is the ego and its illusions, and his method is a prose of metaphor, epigram and abrupt transition that demands a reader's alertness. Modern Love is a sequence of fifty sixteen-line sonnets that narrates the breakdown of a marriage in the third person, and it is the first English poem to treat sexual infidelity from inside both partners. His women — Diana Warwick, Clara Middleton, Carinthia Jane — are among the most intelligent in Victorian fiction, and his theory that comedy is the 'spirit of the social' and a test of conduct made him, for the next generation, the novelist's novelist.
stylistic_characteristics: Epigram, aphorism and the extended metaphor; dialogue that is a contest of wits; abrupt ironic transitions; the 'comic spirit' as a narrator who corrects the characters; a difficult, allusive syntax; the sonnet sequence with a narrative arc.
intellectual_concerns: Egoism and self-deception; marriage, constancy and the war of the sexes; the position of the educated woman; the gentleman as a moral problem; scientific evolution and its social implications; English politics and the aristocratic tradition; comedy as a moral instrument.
historical_significance: Meredith is the finest comic intelligence of Victorian fiction and the writer through whom the Victorian novel passed its most demanding test of intelligence: The Egoist is the classic English comedy of the ego, Modern Love the founding sequence of nineteenth-century poems on marriage, and his criticism of fiction shaped Hardy, Gissing and James. He was the first English novelist to be praised primarily for style, and the 1890s regarded him as their master.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Victorian and Edwardian novel and poetry
literary_identity: Novelist and poet; the last great Victorian novelist and one of the most important English poets of the twentieth century.
biography: Born on 2 June 1840 at Higher Bockhampton, Dorset, son of a builder and stonemason; he was apprenticed to an architect in Dorchester at sixteen and worked in London as an architect's assistant from 1862 to 1867, when ill health returned him to Dorset. Desperate Remedies (1871) began his career; Under the Greenwood Tree (1872), A Pair of Blue Eyes (1873) and Far from the Madding Crowd (1874) established him, and Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895) made him notorious, the latter's reception causing him to abandon fiction for poetry. He married Emma Lavinia Gifford in 1874, and after her death in 1912 made the pilgrimage that produced the 1912-13 poems; he married Florence Dugdale in 1914 and received the Order of Merit in 1910. He died at Max Gate, Dorchester, on 11 January 1928; his heart was buried at Stinsford and his ashes in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: Hardy's novels are set in 'Wessex', a mapped region of the English southwest, and their action is governed by an indifferent universe, by the accidents of time and place, and by the social codes of the rural and small-town world. His method is scenic and ironic: he stages the crucial moments as tableaux, describes landscape and weather with the eye of a painter and the knowledge of a countryman, and observes his characters from a distance that is compassionate and judicial at once. After 1895 he wrote poetry almost exclusively, and the poems — tight, metrically formal, elegiac, often bleak, sometimes bitterly ironic — are among the greatest of the twentieth century, and the 1912-13 poems on his first wife are the central English sequence of grief after In Memoriam.
stylistic_characteristics: Regional landscape used as fate and as a system of signs; the vivid static scene and the dramatic tableau; a narrator's commentary that is ironic and philosophical; chance, coincidence and mis-timed communication as plot machinery; a formal, often archaic diction in the verse; a poetic line that holds tension between the formal measure and the plain statement.
intellectual_concerns: Fate, chance and the indifference of nature; the decline of the rural community; the position of women within marriage and at law; class, ambition and education; desire and its prohibitions; memory and mourning; religion in decline and the persistence of its rituals; the old village and the modern world.
historical_significance: Hardy is the last of the great Victorian novelists and the first great modern English poet of the rural world: Tess and Jude carried Victorian fiction to the edge of the permissible and made him the crucial English novelist of tragedy, and the poems shaped the twentieth-century poetry of landscape, memory and unbelief (Auden, Larkin, Hill all acknowledge him). His Wessex maps made a literary region a permanent imaginative possession, and his influence on the English novel of place is unmatched.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the Victorian adventure romance and the short story
literary_identity: Novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer; the great revivalist of the adventure romance and one of the finest English essayists of the century.
biography: Born in Edinburgh on 13 November 1850, the only child of Thomas Stevenson, a lighthouse engineer. He was educated at Edinburgh Academy and the University of Edinburgh, read law and was called to the bar in 1875, though he never practised. Tuberculosis drove him to travel in search of health: France (1876-79), California (1879-80), where he married Fanny Osbourne in 1880, then Switzerland, the Riviera and Bournemouth. Treasure Island (1883), The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Kidnapped (1886), The Black Arrow (1888), The Master of Ballantrae (1889) and Catriona (1893) made him famous. In 1888 he sailed for the Pacific and settled at Vailima, Samoa, in 1890, where he took the Samoan name Tusitala and intervened in the politics of the islands. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage at Vailima on 3 December 1894 and is buried on Mount Vaea.
literary_profile: Stevenson wrote against the Victorian realist novel: he defended romance, the tale of adventure and the story as craft, and he made the Short Story a serious form in English. His prose is the most perfectly finished of the period — lucid, rhythmic and exact — and his essays on 'A Humble Remonstrance' and 'The Art of Fiction' set out a theory of fiction as a pattern of events rather than a transcript of life. Jekyll and Hyde is his one great myth, a fable of the divided self that became the nineteenth century's most enduring image of the unconscious.
stylistic_characteristics: Classical purity and economy of prose; the carefully planted detail and the withheld explanation; a plot that turns on a single discovery; the Scottish historical novel's vernacular speech; the short story as a designed artefact; the essay as conversation.
intellectual_concerns: The divided self and the beast in man; the romance of adventure and of the boy's initiation; Scottish history, Jacobitism and the Union; travel, exile and the South Seas; honour, loyalty and courage; disease, death and the will to live; the craft of writing.
historical_significance: Stevenson made the adventure romance respectable again after the realists had rejected it, and Jekyll and Hyde is the founding text of modern psychological horror and of the literature of the double. His essays established the short story as a designed form, his South Sea writings are a central document in the critique of imperialism, and his influence on Conrad, Kipling, Borges and the modern story is continuous.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Victorian period, aestheticism and the 1890s
literary_identity: Poet, playwright, novelist, essayist and wit; the central figure of the English aesthetic movement and the greatest comic dramatist of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in Dublin on 16 October 1854, son of Sir William Wilde, surgeon and antiquary, and Jane Francesca Elgee, poet and nationalist. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate prize in 1878 and became a disciple of Pater and Ruskin. After London and a lecture tour of America in 1882 he married Constance Lloyd in 1884 and edited Woman's World (1887-89). The Happy Prince (1888), The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890-91), Lady Windermere's Fan (1892), A Woman of No Importance (1893), An Ideal Husband (1895) and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) followed. His relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas led to his prosecution at Douglas's father's instigation, the trials of April-May 1895 and a sentence of two years' hard labour; he wrote De Profundis in Reading Gaol and The Ballad of Reading Gaol after his release in 1897. He died in Paris on 30 November 1900.
literary_profile: Wilde made the epigram the central English literary form of the 1890s: his comedies are constructed entirely of witty exchanges in which the conventional moral sentence is inverted, and their subject is the hypocrisy of late-Victorian society in matters of marriage, class and reputation. The Picture of Dorian Gray turns the aesthetic doctrine of Pater into a fable of the cost of living for beauty, and De Profundis is the most remarkable Victorian prison letter. His fairy tales and his criticism ('The Decay of Lying', 'The Critic as Artist') argue that art is not a copy of life but the source of it — the most radical statement of the autonomy of art in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram; the comedy of manners with a sudden access of seriousness; the symbolist set-piece and the decorative catalogue; a rhythmic, cadenced prose; the mask and the alias (Bunbury, Ernest); the self-justifying critical dialogue.
intellectual_concerns: Art and its autonomy from morality; appearance and reality; the double life and the secret; marriage and the marriage market; class, manners and the English gentleman; the prison and the outcast; love and its shame; Ireland and the Anglo-Irish position.
historical_significance: Wilde is the central figure of the English aesthetic movement and the greatest writer of comedy after Congreve: The Importance of Being Earnest is the most perfect English farce, Dorian Gray the most perfect English decadent novel, and De Profundis the period's most searching act of self-analysis. His trials made him the Victorian type of the persecuted artist, and his arguments shaped the modern defence of the autonomy of art and the modern gay literary tradition.
biographical_uncertainty: The trials of 1895 are documented in the official record and the newspaper reports; Wilde's own accounts (De Profundis, the letters) are self-interested. The standard biographies are Richard Ellmann (1987) and the Oxford edition of the letters (2000).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian children's literature, nonsense and logic
literary_identity: Writer, logician, mathematician and photographer, born Charles Lutwidge Dodgson; the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and the greatest English writer of literary nonsense.
biography: Born at Daresbury on 27 January 1832, son of a clergyman; educated at Rugby and Christ Church, Oxford, where he matriculated in 1851, became a student (fellow) in 1852 and remained until his death, lecturing in mathematics from 1855 to 1881. He was ordained deacon in 1861 and never proceeded to the priesthood. The Alice stories began as a tale told on 4 July 1862 to Alice Liddell and her sisters during a river excursion; Alice's Adventures in Wonderland appeared in 1865 with Tenniel's illustrations and Through the Looking-Glass in 1871. The Hunting of the Snark (1876), Sylvie and Bruno (1889, 1893) and the mathematical and logical works followed, under his own name. He died at Guildford on 14 January 1898.
literary_profile: Carroll made nonsense a serious literary form: the Alice books are built on the logic of dreams and of language, on puns that turn on the ambiguity of words, on parodies of the Victorian didactic poem, and on a mathematics of inverted rules. He is the first writer for children to treat his reader as an intellectual equal, and his nonsense is not decoration but argument — the reductio ad absurdum of Victorian pedagogy, of the legal system (the Knave's trial), of the schoolroom and the nursery. The later Sylvie and Bruno attempts a fairy tale with a mathematical and theological structure.
stylistic_characteristics: Logical paradox, pun and wordplay; parody of the moralising children's poem; the dream frame and the abrupt transition; invented words (the portmanteau); dialogue driven by the literal reading of a metaphor; mathematical and diagrammatic structures (the chess game of Looking-Glass).
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the adult world's irrationality; language and meaning; rules, games and justice; time, memory and identity; education and its absurdities; the logic of nonsense as a form of moral criticism.
historical_significance: Carroll is the founding figure of English nonsense literature and the most influential children's writer of the century: the Alice books changed what a children's book could be, gave the language 'chortle', 'galumphing' and 'portmanteau', and have been read as philosophy, as mathematics, as political satire and as psychoanalysis. Their influence on Joyce, Eliot, Nabokov and the modern fantastic is direct.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Victorian Gothic and the fin-de-siècle
literary_identity: Novelist, theatre manager and short-story writer; the author of Dracula and the creator of the modern vampire.
biography: Born in Clontarf, Dublin, on 8 November 1847; an invalid in childhood, he was educated at Trinity College Dublin, where he was a mathematician and athlete, and became a civil servant in Dublin Castle. He wrote the theatre column for the Dublin Evening Mail and in 1878 became the business manager of the Lyceum Theatre and Henry Irving's secretary, a post he held until Irving's death in 1905. The Snake's Pass (1890), Dracula (1897), The Jewel of Seven Stars (1903), The Man (1905) and The Lair of the White Worm (1911) followed, together with the stories of Under the Sunset (1881) and the memoir Personal Reminiscences of Henry Irving (1906). He died in London on 20 April 1912.
literary_profile: Stoker wrote the Gothic novel for the age of the typewriter and the medical case study: Dracula is assembled from diaries, letters, newspaper reports, telegrams and 'phonograph' transcripts, its narrative is a montage of documents in the manner Collins had established, and its monster is a figure of the new sciences — of blood transfusion, hypnosis, degeneration and sexual anxiety. The novel's geography runs from the Carpathians to Whitby, London and Transylvania again, and its organisation is that of a league of professional men and one exceptional woman who must hunt the undead.
stylistic_characteristics: Epistolary and documentary collage; the journal and the newspaper report as narrative units; precise medical and legal notation; the eruption of the archaic into the modern city; the use of place and travel; sexual and religious symbolism at the edge of the speakable.
intellectual_concerns: Fear of the foreign and the imperial reverse; sexuality, repression and the Victorian double standard; science, medicine and the new technology; the family and the position of women; empire, race and degeneration; the past returning into the present; superstition against enlightenment.
historical_significance: Dracula is the most influential horror novel ever written and the origin of the modern vampire in literature, film and popular culture. Its documentary method shaped the twentieth-century horror and detective novel, and its figure of the vampire became a permanent instrument for thinking about sexuality, empire and the fear of otherness.
